Development is judged on all three of these together, not on income alone.

1. **Per capita income** is the criterion the World Bank uses to classify countries as rich or low income.
2. **Average literacy level** and **health status** are the education and health indicators that have come to be used along with income as a measure of development.

The Human Development Report published by the UNDP compares countries on exactly these three: the educational levels of the people, their health status and per capita income.

subtopic: How to Compare Different Countries or States
stem: Assume there are four families in a country. The average per capita income of these families is Rs 5000. If the income of three families is Rs 4000, Rs 7000 and Rs 3000 respectively, what is the income of the fourth family?
solution:
**(iv) Rs 6000.**

1. Average income is the total income divided by the number of families, so total income = 5000 x 4 = **Rs 20,000**.
2. Income of the three known families = 4000 + 7000 + 3000 = **Rs 14,000**.
3. Income of the fourth family = 20,000 - 14,000 = **Rs 6,000**.
groundedIn: § How to Compare Different Countries; § Average Income — average income is the total income divided by the total number of people, the rule applied here in reverse to recover the missing family's income

subtopic: How to Compare Different Countries or States
stem: What is the main criterion used by the World Bank in classifying different countries? What are the limitations of this criterion, if any?
solution:
**Per capita income, that is average income, is the main criterion** used by the World Bank in its World Development Reports.

On this basis, countries with a per capita income of US$ 49,300 per annum and above in 2019 are called **high income or rich countries**, and those with US$ 2500 or less are called **low-income countries**. India, at US$ 6700 in 2019, falls in the **low middle income** category.

Limitations:

1. **It hides the distribution of income.** Two countries can have exactly the same average income while one has neither very rich nor extremely poor citizens and the other has four poor citizens and one extremely rich one.
2. **Money cannot buy every good and service people need.** It cannot buy a pollution-free environment or unadulterated medicines, and it cannot protect a person from infectious diseases unless the whole community takes preventive steps.
3. **It ignores other important goals** such as equal treatment, freedom, security and the respect of others.
4. **It can rank a state wrongly.** Haryana has a higher per capita income than Kerala, yet Kerala has a far lower infant mortality rate and a higher literacy rate and net attendance ratio.
groundedIn: § How to Compare Different Countries; § While averages are useful for comparison, they also hide disparities; § Public Facilities — the World Bank's per capita income cut-offs, the comparison of country A with country B, and money not being able to buy a pollution free environment or unadulterated medicines

stem: In what respects is the criterion used by the UNDP for measuring development different from the one used by the World Bank?
solution:
The two differ in the **set of indicators** each uses.

| Basis | World Bank | UNDP |
|---|---|---|
| Criterion | Per capita income alone | Educational levels of the people, their health status and per capita income, taken together |
| Publication | World Development Reports | Human Development Report |
| What it measures | How rich a country is | What is happening to the citizens of a country, that is their health and well being |

By pre-fixing **Human** to Development, the UNDP makes it clear that it is people, their health and their well being that matter most. This is why a country can stand higher on the UNDP's ranking than its income alone would suggest.
groundedIn: § How to Compare Different Countries; § HumanHuman DevelopmentDevelopment; Table 1.6 — the World Bank classifies countries by per capita income while the UNDP report compares them on educational levels, health status and per capita income

subtopic: How to Compare Different Countries or States
stem: Why do we use averages? Are there any limitations to their use? Illustrate with your own examples related to development.
solution:
**We use averages to compare groups that differ in size.**

Countries have different populations, so comparing total income will not tell us what an average person is likely to earn. Dividing the total income of a country by its total population gives the **average income**, also called per capita income, and that can be compared across countries.

Limitations:

1. **An average hides disparities.** It does not tell us how that income is distributed among the people.
2. Take the two countries of Table 1.2. In country A the five citizens earn Rs 9500, Rs 10,500, Rs 9800, Rs 10,000 and Rs 10,200 a month; in country B four earn Rs 500 each and the fifth earns Rs 48,000. **Both have an average income of Rs 10,000**, yet in country A people are neither very rich nor extremely poor while in country B most citizens are poor and one person is extremely rich.
3. Most of us would prefer to live in country A, even though the average says the two are identical. So an average is useful for comparison but is never the whole picture.
groundedIn: § How to Compare Different Countries; § While averages are useful for comparison, they also hide disparities; Table 1.2 — total income cannot tell us what an average person earns, and the two five-citizen countries have identical average income but very different distributions

stem: Kerala, with lower per capita income has a better human development ranking than Haryana. Hence, per capita income is not a useful criterion at all and should not be used to compare states. Do you agree? Discuss.
solution:
**I do not agree**, and this is one defensible position among several.

1. **The example is correct.** Kerala, with a lower per capita income than Haryana, has an infant mortality rate of 7 against Haryana's 30, a literacy rate of 94 per cent against 82, and a net attendance ratio of 83 against 61.
2. **But that makes per capita income insufficient, not useless.** Income is treated as one of the most important attributes for comparing countries, because more income does buy more of many things people need.
3. **Income by itself is not a completely adequate indicator** of the goods and services citizens can actually use, since money cannot buy a pollution-free environment, unadulterated medicines or protection from infectious diseases.
4. **The right conclusion is to use income along with health and education indicators**, as the Human Development Report does, rather than to drop it.
5. Dropping income altogether would also hide real deprivation: Bihar's per capita income of Rs 40,982 against Haryana's Rs 2,36,147 is itself an important fact about how people in Bihar live.
groundedIn: § Income and Other Criteria; § Public Facilities; Table 1.3; Table 1.4 — Haryana's higher per capita income beside Kerala's better infant mortality, literacy and attendance figures, and the chapter's statement that income by itself is not a completely adequate indicator

stem: Find out the present sources of energy that are used by the people in India. What could be the other possibilities fifty years from now?
solution:
**At present India depends largely on non-renewable sources of energy.**

1. **Crude oil** is the example the chapter uses. World reserves in 2017 stood at about 1697 thousand million barrels, enough to last only about **50 years** at the present rate of extraction.
2. **India has to import oil** because it does not have enough stocks of its own, so any rise in oil prices becomes a burden for everyone.

Possibilities fifty years from now:

1. **Renewable sources** such as solar, wind and biogas, which nature replenishes, so that use need not exhaust them.
2. **Newly discovered stocks** of non-renewable resources, since explorations are being undertaken all the time and new sources add to the stock; but even this stock will get exhausted over time.
3. **More careful use of what exists**, because even a renewable resource is overused if we take more than nature replenishes, as is happening with groundwater.
groundedIn: § Sustainability of Development; § Example 2: Exhaustion of — the chapter's renewable and non-renewable distinction, crude oil reserves lasting about 50 years at the present rate of extraction, and India having to import oil because it lacks stocks of its own

stem: Why is the issue of sustainability important for development?
solution:
Sustainability matters because **the level of development a country reaches has to be maintained for future generations**, and since the second half of the twentieth century scientists have been warning that the present type and levels of development are not sustainable.

1. **Renewable resources are being overused.** Groundwater is replenished by rain, yet about 300 districts have reported a water level decline of over 4 metres in the past 20 years, nearly one-third of the country is overusing its groundwater reserves, and 60 per cent would be doing so in another 25 years if present use continues.
2. **Non-renewable resources will be exhausted.** Their stock is fixed and cannot be replenished; crude oil reserves would last only about 50 years at the present rate of extraction.
3. **Environmental damage crosses borders.** Consequences of environmental degradation do not respect national or state boundaries, so the issue is no longer region or nation specific and our future is linked together.
4. Development that destroys the resource base it stands on cannot continue. Sustainability is therefore a condition of development, not an addition to it.
groundedIn: § Sustainability of Development; § Example 1: Groundwater in India — the warning that present levels of development are not sustainable, the groundwater decline figures, and environmental degradation not respecting national or state boundaries

stem: "The Earth has enough resources to meet the needs of all but not enough to satisfy the greed of even one person". How is this statement relevant to the disscusion of development? Discuss.
solution:
The statement means that the earth's resources are enough for everyone's **need** but never enough for anyone's **greed**, and it goes to the heart of the sustainability of development.

1. **Overuse of renewable resources.** Groundwater is replenished by rain, but if we use more than is being replenished we overuse it. About 300 districts have seen the water level fall by over 4 metres in 20 years, and nearly one-third of the country is overusing its reserves.
2. **Exhaustion of non-renewable resources.** Crude oil has a fixed stock that cannot be replenished, and at the present rate of extraction world reserves would last only about 50 years.
3. **Greed leads to conflict.** Countries such as the USA, which have low reserves, want to secure oil through military or economic power.
4. **Need, not greed, must set the level of use.** Development has to be planned so that the present level can at least be maintained for future generations, because we have not inherited the world from our forefathers, we have borrowed it from our children.
groundedIn: § Sustainability of Development; § Example 2: Exhaustion of — the chapter's account of renewable resources being overused beyond what rain replenishes, non-renewable stocks getting exhausted, and countries with low reserves seeking oil through military or economic power

stem: List a few examples of environmental degradation that you may have observed around you.
solution:
Examples of environmental degradation:

1. **A falling water table** caused by overuse of groundwater. About 300 districts have reported a water level decline of over 4 metres in the past 20 years, and the overuse is worst in agriculturally prosperous regions and in rapidly growing urban settlements.
2. **Dumping of toxic waste**, as in the case of the 500 tonnes of liquid toxic waste dumped in open-air dumps and in the surrounding sea at Abidjan.
3. **Polluted air** from such waste. The fumes there caused nausea, skin rashes, fainting and diarrhoea, and within a month seven persons were dead and twenty six thousand were treated for poisoning.
4. **Depletion of non-renewable resources** such as crude oil, whose stock cannot be replenished.

The consequences of all such degradation do not respect national or state boundaries.
groundedIn: § Sustainability of Development; § Example 1: Groundwater in India — the water level decline of over 4 metres in about 300 districts, and the chapter's point that consequences of environmental degradation do not respect national or state boundaries

stem: For each of the items given in Table 1.6, find out which country is at the top and which is at the bottom.
solution:
| Item in Table 1.6 | At the top | At the bottom |
|---|---|---|
| Gross National Income per capita (2017 PPP $) | Sri Lanka, 12,578 | Myanmar, 3,851 |
| Life expectancy at birth | Sri Lanka, 76.4 years | Myanmar, 65.7 years |
| Mean years of schooling of people aged 25 and above | Sri Lanka, 10.8 years | Pakistan, 4.5 years |
| HDI rank in the world (2021-22) | Sri Lanka, rank 73 | Pakistan, rank 161 |

For the HDI, the top position is the **best rank**, which is the lowest number, so Sri Lanka at 73 is at the top and Pakistan at 161 is at the bottom. India is at the top on none of the four items.

| State | Male (%) | Female (%) |
|---|---|---|
| Kerala | 8.5 | 10 |
| Karnataka | 17 | 21 |

| All States | 20 | 23 |
stem: Compare the nutritional level of people in Kerala and Madhya Pradesh.
solution:
**People in Kerala are far better nourished than people in Madhya Pradesh.**

1. Among men, the proportion with a below-normal BMI in Madhya Pradesh is 28 per cent against only 8.5 per cent in Kerala, that is **more than three times** as high.
2. Among women it is 28 per cent against 10 per cent, **nearly three times** as high.
3. Kerala is **below** the all-States figure on both counts (20 per cent male, 23 per cent female), while Madhya Pradesh is **above** it on both.
4. Kerala's position follows from its adequate provision of basic health and educational facilities, the same reason it has the lowest infant mortality rate among the states compared in this chapter.
groundedIn: § Income and Other Criteria; § Public Facilities — Kerala's adequate provision of basic health and educational facilities, which the chapter gives as the reason its health indicators lead

stem: Can you guess why around one-fifth of people in the country are undernourished even though it is argued that there is enough food in the country? Describe in your own words.
solution:
**Because enough food in the country does not mean enough food in every household.**

1. **Income is unequally distributed.** An average hides disparities and does not tell us how income is shared, so a country can show a comfortable average while most of its people are too poor to buy the food they need.
2. **Access depends on public provision.** For many of the important things in life the best and also the cheapest way is to provide them collectively. Where the Public Distribution System functions well the health and nutritional status of the people is certainly likely to be better, and in Tamil Nadu 90 per cent of rural people used a ration shop against only 35 per cent in West Bengal.
3. **Health and education matter as much as the food itself.** Kerala, with adequate basic health and educational facilities, has both the lowest infant mortality rate and the lowest proportion of below-normal BMI.
4. Undernourishment is therefore a problem of **distribution and of public facilities**, not of total supply.
groundedIn: § Public Facilities; § While averages are useful for comparison, they also hide disparities — the Public Distribution System functioning well in some states making health and nutritional status better, and the chapter's point that an average does not tell us how income is distributed among people
